title: Velocity Selectors and Mass Spectrometers
short: Only charges with v = E/B pass straight through crossed fields, and the radius of the path then sorts them by mass-to-charge ratio.
trouble: Students think the selected speed depends on the particle's charge or mass.

blocks.html: A Lorentz force with both an electric and a magnetic part can cancel itself. Arrange $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ at right angles, and for one particular speed the two pushes are equal and opposite. That is the heart of two classic instruments: the velocity selector and the mass spectrometer, which goes on to bend the selected ions into circles.

Velocity selector: with $\vec{E}\perp\vec{B}$, only charges with $$v = \frac{E}{B}$$ pass straight through, whatever their charge or mass.
Mass spectrometer: those charges then enter a field $B'$ alone and circle with radius $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB'}$, so $\dfrac{m}{q} = \dfrac{rB'}{v}$.

Straight through means no net force (Newton's first law): $qE = qvB$. The charge cancels from both sides, and the mass never appears, because nothing is accelerating. A faster particle feels a bigger magnetic force and curves one way; a slower one is pulled the other way by the electric force. Only $v = E/B$ survives the slit at the end. After the selector, every ion has the same speed, so the radius of its circle depends only on $m/q$.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: A velocity selector. Change the speed: too fast, the magnetic force wins; too slow, the electric force wins; at $v = E/B$ the beam flies straight.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: A mass spectrometer: neon-20 and neon-22 ions with the same speed land at different places, because $r = mv/(qB)$.

blocks.title: Choosing a speed
blocks.q: A selector has $E = 2.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{V/m}$ and $B = 0.25\ \text{T}$. Which speed passes?
steps: Electrons, protons and heavy ions all pass at this same speed.

blocks.title: Separating isotopes
blocks.q: Singly charged neon-20 and neon-22 ions ($1\ \text{u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}$) leave that selector and enter a $0.50\ \text{T}$ field, completing half circles. How far apart do they land?
steps: Each lands one diameter from the entrance, so the separation is $2(r_{22} - r_{20}) = 6.64\ \text{mm}$.

blocks.html: "The selected speed depends on the particle's charge or mass." Write the balance: $qE = qvB$. The $q$ divides out, and $m$ is not there at all. A selector set for protons passes electrons of the same speed too (both forces reverse together for negative charge). Charge and mass matter only afterward, in the spectrometer's curve, $r = mv/(qB)$.
In 1897 J. J. Thomson used crossed electric and magnetic fields to measure the charge-to-mass ratio of the particles in cathode rays, the first measurement of a property of the electron.
